topic: restoring a clinker-built wooden dinghy: plank repair, copper fastenings and paint

provenance.author: subagent-en-a
provenance.notes: independent English scenario, not a translation; five sentences per turn

a: I have measured six planks on the port side in millimetres: 210, 195, 188, 205, 199 and 212.
Sort those widths from narrowest to widest and keep them in millimetres as whole numbers.
Give me the mean width to one decimal place and the spread between the extremes.
Then tell me which planks are more than five millimetres away from that mean width.
Convert the mean into inches to two decimal places, using twenty-five point four per inch.
base: The dinghy is clinker built, about fourteen feet, and has been under a tarpaulin for nine years.
Three planks near the waterline are soft, and one has split along the line of the fastenings.
The rest of the hull looks sound, though the paint has lifted almost everywhere.
I want to keep as much original wood as I can, rather than replank the whole side.
Where does it make sense to start with a hull that has been left in that state?

a: Sorted from narrowest to widest the six planks run 188, 195, 199, 205, 210 and 212.
The mean width is 201.5 millimetres and the spread between the extremes is 24 millimetres.
Four planks lie more than five millimetres from the mean, namely 188, 195, 210 and 212.
The two inside that band are 199 and 205, both within four millimetres of the mean.
In inches the mean width is 7.93, using twenty-five point four millimetres to the inch.
base: Start by finding out how far the softness runs, because the paint hides the real edge of it.
Push a bradawl into the plank every hand's width and mark where it stops going in easily.
Nine years under a tarpaulin usually means water sat in one place rather than everywhere.
The split plank is a separate matter, and a scarfed graving piece may be enough there.
How are the planks fastened, copper rivets through the lands or nails clenched over?

a: I have four boxes of copper rivets holding 120, 85, 240 and 60 pieces.
Add those up and tell me how many rivets I have in total across the four boxes.
Each land needs a rivet every seventy millimetres along a plank of two thousand millimetres.
Work out how many rivets one land takes, rounding up to the nearest whole rivet.
Then tell me how many full lands I can fasten with the rivets I already hold.
base: They are copper rivets through the lands, with roves on the inside, and most look sound.
A handful near the split have gone green and one or two have worked loose.
I would rather not disturb the ones that are still tight, if that is defensible.
The soft area runs about a metre and a half along two planks, judging by the bradawl.
Below that the wood stays hard all the way down to the garboard plank.

a: The four boxes hold 505 rivets in total, adding 120, 85, 240 and 60 together.
One land of two thousand millimetres takes 29 rivets, once the spacing is rounded up.
Dividing 505 by 29 gives 17 full lands, with 12 rivets left over.
That is enough for seventeen lands and not quite enough for an eighteenth.
The leftover twelve rivets will cover repairs but not a further full land.
base: Leaving tight rivets alone is standard practice, so long as you can reach the roves.
Cut out the soft length as a long tapered patch rather than a square hole.
A metre and a half is well within what a graving piece can carry safely.
Match the grain direction and the thickness, and bed it on flexible sealant.
The garboard being hard is good news, because that plank is the worst one to renew.

a: The hull has an area of about eighteen square metres above and below the waterline.
One litre of primer covers eight square metres and one litre of topcoat covers ten.
Work out how much primer I need for one coat and how much topcoat for two coats.
Round both figures up to the nearest half litre, and give them in litres.
Then add the two together, for a single total of paint to order.
base: Once the wood is sound I need to think about what goes on the outside.
The old paint is a hard gloss that has gone brittle and lifts in sheets.
I do not know whether to strip back to bare wood or feather the edges.
Traditional soft paint would suit the boat, though it needs doing more often.
Does the choice change anything about how I finish the repaired planks?

a: One coat of primer over eighteen square metres needs 2.25 litres, which rounds to 2.5.
Two coats of topcoat cover thirty-six square metres and need 3.6 litres, rounding to 4.
That gives 2.5 litres of primer and 4 litres of topcoat, both rounded up.
The single order total is 6.5 litres of paint for the whole hull.
Both figures are given in litres, rounded to the nearest half litre as asked.
base: Strip back to bare wood on the repaired area, and feather the sound paint around it.
A brittle gloss will keep lifting under anything you put over the top of it.
Soft paint is kinder to a clinker hull, because it moves with the planks.
It also lets water out of the wood instead of trapping it under a hard skin.
Whichever you choose, prime the new wood twice before the first full coat.

a: Here is the tool list: block plane, spokeshave, bradawl, rivet set, clenching iron and scraper.
Sort those tools into shaping tools and fastening tools, keeping the order they appear in.
Put the scraper with the shaping tools and the bradawl with the fastening tools.
Then count each group and give me the two totals on one line.
Do not list any tool in both groups and do not add anything new.
base: That makes sense, and it fits the way the boat was built in the first place.
I have most of the hand tools already, apart from a proper clenching iron.
The rivet set I have is worn on one face and may bruise the copper.
Working single handed is the other problem, since riveting really wants two pairs of hands.
Is there a way to hold the roves without a second person on the inside?

a: The shaping tools are the block plane, the spokeshave and the scraper, in that order.
The fastening tools are the bradawl, the rivet set and the clenching iron, in that order.
That is three tools in the shaping group and three tools in the fastening group.
The scraper sits with the shaping tools and the bradawl with the fastening tools, as asked.
No tool appears twice and nothing has been added to the original list.
base: A heavy dolly held against the rove will do the work of a second pair of hands.
Clamp it to a batten so it stays put while you strike from the outside.
Dress the worn face of the rivet set flat before you use it on the copper.
A bruised rove never seats properly and will weep for the life of the plank.
Work along the land in short runs rather than trying to finish a whole plank.

a: Write out the repair steps in order, from cutting the patch to the final coat.
Number them from one to seven and keep each step on a single short line.
Mark which steps have to wait for something to dry before the next one starts.
Then list the three steps that need a second pair of hands, in the same order.
Keep it plain and do not add any explanation between the numbered steps.
base: That gives me a way through it, working plank by plank rather than all at once.
The season is the last thing on my mind, and it is already the end of March.
I would like her afloat by July, which leaves about three months of evenings.
The real worry is whether the repaired planks will take up when she goes in.
She was always a dry boat before, but that was nine years and one tarpaulin ago.

a: The repair steps run: cut the patch, fit it dry, bed it, rivet it, plane it fair, prime, paint.
Steps three, six and seven have to wait for bedding compound or paint to dry.
That drying time sets the pace of the whole job more than the cutting does.
Steps two, four and five want a second pair of hands, in that order.
The list is set out plain, with nothing added in between the numbered steps.
base: Three months of evenings is enough, provided the bedding and paint get their drying time.
Planks that have dried for nine years will take up, but they will weep at first.
Put her in on a rising tide with a pump aboard and give her two days.
Keep the bilge wet for a week rather than hauling out at the first sign of water.
A clinker hull tightens as the wood swells, and the rivets do the rest.
